newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German government riven by tax conflicts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German government riven by tax conflicts.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling government coalition looked increasingly brittle on Monday as an embarassing rift refused to heal over tax increases it might yet need to implement ahead of European monetary union.

Kohl himself had to step in to tell some of his most senior government members to stop bickering in public after Finance Minister Theo Waigel provoked a cabinet colleague into a slanging match over Germany's tottering public finances.

The row came as another government figure hinted that a deal could come with opposition politicians on a major tax reform due for next year, a move which could enrage the junior coalition partners Kohl needs for his parliamentary majority.

Waigel had walked into controversy at the weekend by accusing other government departments of ruining his budget sums in the qualification year for the single European currency by offering him botched economic forecasts.

The comments immediately provoked Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, a member of the Free Democrats (FDP) who prop up Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) in parliament, into a stinging rebuke of Waigel for using a "transparent manoeuvre to distract from his own faults".

Continuing the assault on Waigel in Paris, where he was attending OECD ministerial talks on Monday, Rexrodt said Waigel was above all wrong to blame his ministry because forecasts on the economy were the result of cross-ministry work.

Kohl, himself taking no position on whether Germany would need to raise taxes to ensure it meets Maastricht criteria for European economic and monetary union, said calm discussion rather than public rowing was in order.
"Let's talk to each other first before we start talking about each other," Kohl told journalists at a meeting of CDU executives in Bonn.
He said the 1998 budget and the question of whether there was a need for a mini-budget this year would all be on the agenda of formal budget discussions due on July 2.

Government heayweights had earlier on Monday leapt to defend Waigel, with CDU general secretary Peter Hintze accusing the free-market FDP of losing all touch with reality by insisting that Waigel rule out tax rises to help the budget.

"You cannot simply substitute oaths for the rules of mathematics," Hintze said on German radio, referring to the FDP's newly-agreed party resolution excluding any rise in taxes to plug budget shortfalls.

The FDP, at a weekend party conference, adopted a motion opposing tax increases and insisting the Kohl coalition stick to a deal to cut the solidarity surcharge -- a tax raised to help pay for German unification -- by two points next year.
The FDP is above all adamant that the planned tax reform, due to come into effect from 1998, deliver all the 30 billion marks ($17.8 billion) of tax cuts currently promised.

But those promises were thrown into doubt in April when the SPD, which controls the upper house of parliament and whose support the government was seeking, pulled out of talks aimed at getting cross-party support for the reform.

But Wolfgang Schaeuble, CDU parliamentary leader, told a news briefing that he saw some positive aspects in a new SPD plan, which unlike current government proposals sets out a budget-neutral restructuring of the tax system.
"(There are) some starting positions for a quick agreement," Schaeuble told a news briefing called directly after an SPD conference unveiling its tax plans.
Earlier, the SPD set out proposals to restructure some 78 billion marks of revenues in the tax system, giving tax breaks to families and workers while raising revenues elsewhere.

SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine however continued to insist that a reduction in the 53-percent tax bracket was only possible if it could be financed elsewhere. He added the government's plans to cut the top tax bracket to 39 percent could not be financed.
Waigel, while accusing Lafontaine of mere "crowd-pleasing", insisted the government was nonetheless ready to restart talks with the SPD any time.

"We are ready at any time to hold talks with the SPD. It would be good if they took place in July, August or the first half of September," Waigel told reporters before giving a speech in Duesseldorf. ($1.685= German Marks)
